clue.text: Utilitarian, crooked, indifferent actor, puts on new tie

parts.note: crooked means bent, as in dishonest or out of true
a poor, overacting performer is a ham

indicators.note: new signals that the letters of the word tie are made afresh in another order

explanation.surface: A practical-minded person, a dodgy and second-rate performer, dresses up in a fresh necktie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' turns TIE into ITE. A Utilitarian follows Jeremy Bentham, the philosopher of the greatest happiness of the greatest number.
explanation.definitionFit: Followers of Jeremy Bentham's philosophy are named after him, and his doctrine is utilitarianism.

clue.text: Updike protagonist who returned

parts.note: John Updike's novelist hero came back in a sequel titled with his name followed by 'Is Back'

explanation.walkthrough: Henry Bech, the writer-hero of Updike's 'Bech: A Book', returned in 'Bech Is Back'.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Bech is John Updike's fictional novelist, star of three story collections including one announcing his comeback.

clue.text: Black Italian violinist

explanation.surface: A dark-clad musician from Italy plays the fiddle.
explanation.walkthrough: The Italian word for black is nero; the Roman emperor Nero is said to have fiddled while Rome burned.
explanation.definitionFit: Italian for black is nero, and the emperor of legend played the fiddle as his city blazed.

clue.text: "No less 'necessary and right are the brutalities of men in brown shirts " (Aldous Huxley, Ends and Means)

definitions.text: "No less 'necessary and right are the brutalities of men in brown shirts " (Aldous Huxley, Ends and Means)

parts.words: "No less 'necessary and right are the brutalities of men in brown shirts " (Aldous Huxley, Ends and Means)
parts.note: a quotation with a gap after 'No less', to be filled with the adverb Huxley wrote there

explanation.walkthrough: The printed clue lost the dash marking the gap after 'No less'; Huxley's sentence reads 'No less historically necessary and right...', mocking the claim that history justifies violence.
explanation.definitionFit: Huxley's adverb says the violence was justified in terms of the course of past events.

clue.text: Intended to provide me with a sacred book

parts.note: NT is the New Testament, the Christian sacred book

explanation.surface: Someone was destined to be handed a holy text.
explanation.walkthrough: ME, then A and NT (New Testament); the printed clue as filed lacks the 'a' the wordplay needs.
explanation.definitionFit: What you had in mind to do is what you aimed or purposed to do.

clue.text: Muir poem extended by Cary?

explanation.surface: A Scottish poet's verse gets lengthened by a novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: Edwin Muir wrote the poem 'The Horses'; Joyce Cary's novel 'The Horse's Mouth' adds a word to the title, so Cary extended it.
explanation.definitionFit: Edwin Muir's post-apocalyptic poem has this title, and it begins the title of Joyce Cary's novel about a painter.

clue.text: Singer revealed many in total here

indicators.note: in says the letter for many sits within the word for total

parts.note: a total is a sum
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, so many

explanation.surface: A vocalist exposed the large number of people present.
explanation.walkthrough: Singer here is Isaac Bashevis Singer, not a vocalist: his late novel 'Scum' revealed the Warsaw underworld.
explanation.definitionFit: Isaac Bashevis Singer's novel of 1991 bears this title, depicting a seedy world he laid bare.

clue.text: Plural gerundive putting matters to rights

definitions.text: Plural gerundive putting matters to rights

parts.words: Plural gerundive putting matters to rights
parts.note: a Latin neuter plural gerundive meaning 'things to be corrected', used for a list of fixes

explanation.walkthrough: The Latin gerundive of corrigere, to correct, gives the word for a list of errors to be put right in a book.
explanation.definitionFit: A Latin plural meaning 'things to be corrected', it names the list of errata inserted into a printed book.

clue.text: Banks's man

parts.note: Isabella Banks wrote a Victorian novel about a man named after a Lancashire city

explanation.walkthrough: Mrs G. Linnaeus Banks wrote 'The Manchester Man' (1876); the clue drops the city.
explanation.definitionFit: Isabella Banks's best-known novel is titled for a man of this northern English city.

clue.text: Unexpectedly ablest rich girl portrayed by Coleridge

indicators.note: unexpectedly signals the letters of ablest rich come out in a surprising order

explanation.surface: Surprisingly, the most capable wealthy young woman was depicted by a Romantic poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Coleridge's unfinished narrative poem is named for its heroine, a lady enchanted by Geraldine.

clue.text: Dramatist's islands in far Antarctic

indicators.note: in says the answer sits within the words far Antarctic

explanation.surface: A playwright's islands lie in the remote Antarctic.
explanation.walkthrough: J. M. Synge wrote 'The Aran Islands' about the islands off Ireland's west coast, nowhere near the Antarctic.
explanation.definitionFit: Synge's prose book describes the three Irish islands in Galway Bay where he stayed.

clue.text: Bates's high regard for daily chaos?

parts.note: high regard is love
taken as written

indicators.note: chaos says the letters of daily are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: A writer's great esteem for a newspaper in disarray.
explanation.walkthrough: 'chaos' turns DAILY into LYDIA. H. E. Bates wrote the novel 'Love for Lydia' (1952).
explanation.definitionFit: H. E. Bates's novel of youthful passion in the 1920s carries this title, so it is Bates's book.

clue.text: Firm defender of Solzhenitsyn suggests provost confused about love in rich surroundings

indicators.note: in rich surroundings means the word rich encloses everything else

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: about means the jumbled letters go round the letter for love
confused says the letters of provost are jumbled

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: A loyal supporter of the Russian dissident hints that a muddled college head is wrapped in love amid luxury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confused' turns PROVOST into OSTRPOV; 'about' puts it round O, giving OSTROPOV; 'in rich surroundings' puts that inside R...ICH. The cellist Mstislav Rostropovich sheltered Solzhenitsyn.
explanation.definitionFit: The cellist Mstislav Rostropovich gave the dissident novelist refuge at his dacha and publicly defended him.

clue.text: Many a verse, both short and terse, may well be worse, without this curse

definitions.text: Many a verse, both short and terse, may well be worse, without this curse

parts.words: Many a verse, both short and terse, may well be worse, without this curse
parts.note: every line of the clue ends on the same rhyme sound, demonstrating the device it describes

explanation.walkthrough: The clue itself uses a single rhyme throughout: verse, terse, worse, curse.
explanation.definitionFit: Poems in which all lines share one rhyme are named for that single repeated sound.

clue.text: Slimmer spa transformed for elderly spinster

indicators.note: transformed signals that the letters of slimmer spa are made over into a new word

explanation.surface: A dieter's health resort is remade for an old unmarried woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Agatha Christie's village sleuth Jane Marple is the archetypal elderly spinster.
explanation.definitionFit: Agatha Christie's amateur detective is an unmarried old lady from St Mary Mead.

clue.text: "My aunt and her paramour … such a pair of —, as I believe, all England could not parallel" (Smollett, Humphrey Clinker)

definitions.text: "My aunt and her paramour … such a pair of —, as I believe, all England could not parallel" (Smollett, Humphrey Clinker)

parts.words: "My aunt and her paramour … such a pair of —, as I believe, all England could not parallel" (Smollett, Humphrey Clinker)
parts.note: a quotation with a dash for the missing plural noun Smollett used for two unique eccentrics

explanation.walkthrough: Fill the gap from Smollett's novel: the aunt and her lover are a pair of eccentrics without parallel.
explanation.definitionFit: Eccentric people unlike anyone else are called this, and the quotation stresses that no match exists in England.

clue.text: Imagist noting lad has changed

indicators.note: has changed says the letters of noting lad have been altered into another order

explanation.surface: A poet notices that a boy is different.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Aldington was one of the Imagist poets, alongside H.D. and Ezra Pound.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Aldington belonged to the early twentieth-century poetry movement led by Pound.

clue.text: They are apparently ruled out in Dick Francis's Odds Against

definitions.text: They are apparently ruled out in Dick Francis's Odds Against

parts.words: They are apparently ruled out in Dick Francis's Odds Against
parts.note: a novel's title about betting prices seems to exclude the price of one to one

explanation.walkthrough: Betting odds can be 'against' or at an even price; a title of 'odds against' would seem to exclude even money. Dick Francis wrote racing thrillers.
explanation.definitionFit: A one-to-one betting price is called this, which is neither odds on nor odds against.

clue.text: Musical alternative in loss Iago suffered ()

indicators.note: in says the answer is sitting inside the words loss Iago

explanation.surface: Iago's tragic downfall in the opera.
explanation.walkthrough: Ossia, Italian for 'or else', marks an alternative passage in a score.
explanation.definitionFit: In printed music an optional easier or different passage is marked with this Italian word meaning 'or'.

clue.text: The long, slow feet of M-M-Morse

definitions.text: The long, slow feet of M-M-Morse

parts.words: The long, slow feet of M-M-Morse
parts.note: in Morse code M is two dashes, so M-M is four long marks, like a metrical foot of four long syllables

explanation.walkthrough: A spondee is a foot of two long syllables; the doubled foot has four longs, as the two Morse Ms (dash-dash, dash-dash) show. The stammer also suggests slowness.
explanation.definitionFit: In prosody a double spondee, four long syllables in a row, gets this name.

clue.text: Peacock's hasty passage

parts.note: hasty means headlong, rushing without thought
a hall is a passage or corridor

explanation.surface: A bird's hurried dash down a corridor.
explanation.walkthrough: Peacock is Thomas Love Peacock, author of the satirical novel 'Headlong Hall' (1816), not the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Love Peacock's first novel, a satire set at a Welsh country house, bears this title.

clue.text: Tritten tracked her maturity ()

parts.note: Charles Tritten wrote a sequel following Johanna Spyri's Swiss girl as she grows up

explanation.walkthrough: Charles Tritten, Spyri's translator, wrote 'Heidi Grows Up' and 'Heidi's Children'.
explanation.definitionFit: Johanna Spyri's Alpine orphan girl was given sequels by Tritten showing her as an adult.

clue.text: Italian author was something of a volatile visionary

indicators.note: something of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: An Italian writer had something of the restless dreamer about him.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft put 'was' in the definition, but 'Italian author was' cannot stand for a name; 'was' is a link. Primo Levi wrote 'If This Is a Man'.
explanation.definitionFit: Primo Levi, the Turin chemist and Auschwitz survivor, was a celebrated Italian writer.

clue.text: Given self-regard, given name: given name, expressionist

parts.note: the ego is one's self-regard

explanation.surface: A self-absorbed person with a first name takes on a forename belonging to an Expressionist painter.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated 'given' is wordplay glue; the definition is the forename of the Austrian Expressionist Egon Schiele.
explanation.definitionFit: The Austrian Expressionist painter Schiele's first name, the one he was christened with.

clue.text: Bentley said geography was about them

definitions.text: Bentley said geography was about them

parts.words: Bentley said geography was about them
parts.note: E. C. Bentley's clerihew contrasts geography, which is about charts, with biography, which is about chaps

explanation.walkthrough: Bentley invented the clerihew; one runs 'Geography is about maps, / But Biography is about chaps.'
explanation.definitionFit: Bentley's clerihew says geography concerns charts of the land, while biography concerns people.

clue.text: Dr. rents big new construction for playwright

indicators.note: new construction says the letters of dr rents big are built into another shape

explanation.surface: A doctor lets out a large new building for a dramatist.
explanation.walkthrough: August Strindberg was the Swedish dramatist of 'Miss Julie'.
explanation.definitionFit: August Strindberg, the Swedish author of 'Miss Julie' and 'The Father', wrote plays.

clue.text: Let it remain in Durrell's tetralogy

indicators.note: in says the answer is lodged inside the words Durrell's tetralogy

explanation.surface: Leave it inside the Alexandria Quartet.
explanation.walkthrough: Lawrence Durrell's tetralogy is the Alexandria Quartet; stet is the proofreader's Latin for 'let it stand'.
explanation.definitionFit: Proofreaders write this Latin word to cancel a correction and keep the original text.

clue.text: Nabokov issued one — to see a production of Murdoch's A Severed Head?

definitions.text: Nabokov issued one — to see a production of Murdoch's A Severed Head?

parts.words: Nabokov issued one — to see a production of Murdoch's A Severed Head?
parts.note: Nabokov's novel title ends 'to a Beheading', and a stage show of Murdoch's novel would be a sort of beheading to watch

explanation.walkthrough: Nabokov wrote 'Invitation to a Beheading'; Iris Murdoch's 'A Severed Head' was adapted for the stage, so going to see it is a beheading in a sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A request to attend an event is this, as in Nabokov's novel title about a beheading.
